Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Department of Justice’s Office of Professional Responsibility—its internal ethics watchdog—on Tuesday revealed that it has referred two of its attorneys for potential bar discipline over their use of artificial intelligence in doing their jobs.

The lawyers’ professional conduct concerns included disclosing confidential documents to a public AI platform and ‌making misleading statements to a judge when discussing how AI-generated errors appeared in a court filing, according to a story by Reuters.

Neither lawyer is named in the report.

The lawyers have been referred to the DOJ’s Professional Misconduct Review Unit, which can then make recommendations to state bar authorities, according to a story by Bloomberg Law.

Cravath, Swaine & Moore’s associate salary scale was increased Tuesday, and it rivals the raises announced in June at Milbank, according to coverage by Reuters.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • (CN) â With the United States a climate-denying no-show and the European Union retreating on climate leadership, the annual United Nations climate summit veered toward failure Friday.
  • The summit, known as COP31, was on the brink of becoming a massive disappointment with civil society groups calling it the worst U.N.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that developing nations and activists are furious over a lack of pledges to phase out fossil fuels and boost climate funding in a draft declaration from this yearâs U.N. climate summit.Â.

(CN) â With the United States a climate-denying no-show and the European Union retreating on climate leadership, the annual United Nations climate summit veered toward failure Friday.

The summit, known as COP31, was on the brink of becoming a massive disappointment with civil society groups calling it the worst U.N. climate summit in history and Panama’s negotiator saying the world was âbeing held hostage by the petroleum mafia.â.

The two-week summit â held this year in Antalya, Turkey â formally ended Friday, but negotiations on the wording of a final declaration were set to stretch into the weekend.

Huge divisions opened up Thursday after richer nations, led by the European Union, offered paltry sums to help developing countries fight climate change and oil-producing countries managed to strip language about phasing out fossil fuels from a draft text of a final declaration.

âWithout any doubt, this has been the worst COP ever,â mentioned Mohamed Adow, the head of Power Shift Africa, at a news conference Friday held by the Climate Action Network, a global civil society coalition.

Tasneem Essop, the executive director of Climate Action Network, remarked there was ânothing on the table that protects people or addresses the priorities of the Global South.â.

Anger was directed at the EU for backing away from pledges to provide poorer countries with large sums of money to deal with climate change.

On the eve of the summit, Wopke Hoekstra, the EU’s climate commissioner, said new financial commitments were âdead in the water.â.

Sources indicate that âThink about that,â Essop, a South African, said. âDead in the water. For us in the Global South, dead in the water is very literal.â.

By Friday, richer countries had pledged only about $50 million into a fund to help countries adapt to climate change.

But that amounted to only one-sixth of an annual target of $300 million agreed to at last year’s climate summit in BelÃ©m, Brazil, and fell well short of a broader goal to mobilize $1.2 billion from 2026 to 2029.

Recent findings suggest that the EU rejected the criticism with its officials arguing the bloc provides the lionâs share of global climate finance. Last year, the EU and its 27 member states provided about $35 billion in public sources to support developing countries deal with climate change, according to an EU news release.

But developing nations blasted the lack of new commitments at the summit from wealthier countries.

It has been revealed that âWe didnât come here to beg,â remarked Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, the lead negotiator for African nations. âWe came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries.â.

Many delegates and activists blamed European countries for blocking progress in other areas too.

In recent years, the EU has backed away from leading on climate issues in the face of domestic backlash against its ambitious climate goals.

Europe’s retreat on climate stems from weak industrial output, the rise of far-right parties, a cost-of-living crisis and the climate skepticism of U.S. President Donald Trump.

Recent findings suggest that for a second year in a row, the U.S. did not send a delegation to the climate summit, a move that severely undermined the talks.

Upon returning to the White House in 2025, Trump removed the U.S. from the 2015 Paris climate accord, and thereby withdrew one of the world’s top emitters from the international framework to reduce carbon emissions.

In Turkey, delegations and activists were dismayed at the removal of language calling for the phase-out of fossil fuels.

Instead, the draft declaration put emphasis on boosting electrification around the world and supporting technologies to remove carbon from the atmosphere.

In a recent development, the draft text called for increasing electricity’s share of global energy use from 23% to 35% by 2035. This pledge was almost certain to remain in the final text and become the summit’s main theme.

But even this pledge was criticized for not saying renewable energy sources should be favored over fossil fuels in this electrification drive.

The final text likely will include support for carbon capture and storage technology, but critics remarked it remains an unproven means of reducing greenhouse gases.

Australia and Turkey jointly presided over the negotiations and argued the summit had made progress.

In a recent development, murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister and summit co-president, noted it was not necessary to call for a phase-out of fossil fuels because that language had been included in previous COP declarations. In 2023, a climate summit in Dubai called for phasing out fossil fuels, but since then the climate talks largely have avoided the topic.

âI do not think we are taking a step back,â Kurum said. âI think the determined steps we have taken need to be supported. It is clear we cannot get anywhere by repeating the same discussions.â.

Fears over artificial intelligence have come to a head, causing tech stocks to plunge and the Nasdaq to lose all its gains for the year in mere days.

MANHATTAN (CN) â Investors and economists have warned for weeks about an artificial intelligence bubble.

This weekâs sell-off may be the payoff to that prediction.

By the closing bell on Friday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 4,199 points and the S&P 500 fell 651 points, both verging on market corrections. The Nasdaq had a pretty bad week, too, falling 2,519 points.

Analysts warn the carnage may not be over.

It has been revealed that âWe think the falls in tech stocks and the S&P 500 have further to run,â James Reilly, senior markets economist at Capital Economics, wrote in an investorâs note. “How this plays out within the stock market will depend on what is driving these falls.â.

It has been revealed that earlier in the week, investors were temporarily pleased with Nvidiaâs positive earnings, which indicated third-quarter revenue beat expectations by $6 billion and more than 100% higher than a year ago. Nvidiaâs revenue is also more than double what it was the same time in 2025, despite former CEO Jensen Huangâs scandalous departure last week.

According to recent reports, even with some calling for Huangâs return, the firm seems well-poised to move on without him. âOur momentum is real,â interim CEO Colette Kress stated in the companyâs earnings release. âOur roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater.â.

Not even the record-breaking initial public offering from Anthropic this week helped tech stocks, as shares of Anthropic fell more than 11% since its inception on Thursday.

Beyond tech stocks, other data this week showed mixed signals for the economy.

The monthly consumer sentiment survey from the University of Michigan increased slightly over October and now is roughly where it stood on November 2025. All of the surveyâs index components increased, with short-term expected business conditions increasing 13% over the last month and expectations for gas prices over the next year falling to their lowest reading since February.

It has been revealed that âCurrent personal finances improved from last month for middle- and low-wealth consumers, who felt some relief stemming from recent declines in gas prices,â the surveyâs director Joanne Hsu stated in a statement. âIn contrast, those with the largest stockholdings reported a decline, consistent with this monthâs agitation in stock markets.â.

Not surprisingly, a growing number of respondents mentioned a potential AI bubble, as well as concerns about its effect on labor markets.

Retail sales came in roughly as expected, but the 0.2% increase in sales for October was far less than then 0.8% seen for September. Still, experts point to the report as evidence consumers are not afraid to keep spending.

According to recent reports, the reason for the drop from September is likely due to the fall in gasoline station spending, since oil prices have come down in the last several weeks. Exclude autos and gasoline, though, and retail sales increased by 0.5% last month.

Other areas showed strength. Online spending and restaurant spending continue apace, at a 12% annualized increase and 7% annualized increase, respectively. Health and personal care stores also saw a 1.5% monthly gain in sales.

âAs long as consumers continue to spend and the economy keeps growing, then profits will grow as well, and markets will eventually find their footing and begin moving higher again,â said Chris Zacarelli, chief investment officer at Northlight Asset Management.

Other data shows the economy slowing. The Empire State Manufacturing Survey showed an 18-point drop to 7.8, compared with the expectation it would drop only to 16. While the surveyâs general business conditions index remained positive at 7.8, it also fell slightly.

In a recent development, on the plus side, the surveyâs employment measure expanded at the fastest pace seen in more than four years. Respondent firms are more optimistic about economic conditions improving in the upcoming months.

    On Friday, a Ninth Circuit panel revived Shillingâs lawsuit against Martinez, finding a lower court erred in dismissing the action against the sheriff and San Diego County.

    Shilling received his license to carry concealed weapons in June 2022 under the previous sheriff. However, his license was revoked by Martinez in December 2023 under a clause in the California penal code requiring âgood moral character.".

    Sources indicate that writing in a unanimous decision, U.S. Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay found that Shilling sufficiently claimed his right to free association had been infringed after the sheriff deprived him of his Second Amendment right.

While preventing an individual from participating in a groupâs lawful activities may be one way to violate the First Amendment right, itâs infringed in âvaried ways.ââ.

    The three-judge panel found Martinez was acting as a policymaker, rather than a state official, in her revocation of Shillingâs license under the good moral character requirement.

    Recent findings suggest that âNo state law mandated this county-specific definition,â Bumatay continued. âIn other words, the county of San Diego â not California â made association with the Boozefighters a basis to revoke a CCW license.â.

    According to recent reports, bumatay was joined by U.S. Circuit Judge Kenneth Lee, another Trump appointee, and U.S. Circuit Judge Jennifer Sung, a Joe Biden appointee.

    “The Bill of Rightâs prevails over politics,” attorney Gary Gorski, representing Shilling, said in an email to Courthouse News.

    The good moral character requirement in the stateâs penal code was replaced with more objective and defined criteria in January 2024, shortly after the revocation of Shillingâs license, following the Supreme Courtâs decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen.

    Shilling filed the lawsuitin June 2024.

    Recent findings suggest that in his complaint, he described the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club as an organization that is more involved in charitable events than its historical status might suggest. The organization was founded in Los Angeles in 1946 by returning World War II veterans seeking camaraderie over their shared love of motorcycle riding.

    The organization states it has never been an outlaw motorcycle gang or part of the â1%â of motorcycle clubs that operate outside mainstream riding activities.

    In a recent development, shilling, a resident of Chula Vista, California, has been a longtime employee at the Chula Vista Elementary School District. He has no criminal history, the panel wrote.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Courthousenews

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Omaha-based National Indemnity sued, saying the reinsurer did not fully cover its losses after Montana failed to warn of the dangers in and around the small city of Libby.
    • According to recent reports, OMAHA, Neb.
    • Jurors found National Indemnity complied with its obligations under the reinsurance certificate and proved its breach of contract claim against TIG.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Omaha-based National Indemnity sued, saying the reinsurer did not fully cover its losses after Montana failed to warn of the dangers in and around the small city of Libby.

    According to recent reports, OMAHA, Neb. (CN) â An eight-person federal jury found reinsurer TIG liable after Omaha-based National Indemnity claimed TIG didn’t fully cover a sweeping payout for widespread contamination from the Libby Mine asbestos exposure.

    Jurors found National Indemnity complied with its obligations under the reinsurance certificate and proved its breach of contract claim against TIG. They awarded National Indemnity $39.2 million in indemnity, $3.2 million in prejudgment interest, $21.1 million in postjudgment interest and $16.1 million in expenses.

    They declined to award National Indemnity any future defense costs.

    Attorneys for both sides declined to comment after the verdict was read.

    National Indemnity Insurance Organization turned to TIG Insurance Company and other reinsurers after agreeing in 2022, with Montana, to resolve all coverage claims over asbestos exposure from the mine since the 1960s for $157 million.

    National Indemnity insured the state from July 1, 1973, to July 1, 1975; TIG provided the company’s reinsurance at that time.

    TIG claimed National Indemnity did not offer adequate evidence and billed amounts not covered by the reinsurance agreement, essentially finagling the numbers to make TIG cover part of the massive bill.

    âIt lied," remarked Scott L. Davis, a Dallas-based attorney for the Spencer Fane firm, representing TIG, speaking of National Indemnity during closing arguments late Thursday afternoon.

    National Indemnity mentioned it kept TIG informed throughout the claims process, but the reinsurer never got involved, something it had a right to do.

    Industry observers note that “They could have helped; they didnât,” Michael Knoerzer, a New York-based attorney for Clyde & Co., representing National Indemnity, told the jury Thursday. âItâs undisputed in this case they never asked.â.

    In 2004, the state of Montana was found liable for asbestos risk to miners and residents near Libby, a small city in the state’s northwest.

    In a recent development, from 1963 to 1990, W.R. Grace & Co. extracted vermiculite at the mine, about 7 miles outside of Libby. Vermiculite, once commonly used for fireproof roofing, insulation and wallpaper, is not dangerous. But the asbestos the mining stirred up was.

    Industry observers note that decades of widespread asbestos contamination from the mine caused the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to declare its first-ever public health emergency during a 2009 Superfund cleanup.

    In a recent development, thousands of W.R. Grace workers, their families and residents since the 1960s have been injured or died from lung disease related to working at or living near the mine.

    Industry observers note that the fight over who should be held liable started about 2000, shortly after reports of workers falling ill sparked an emergency cleanup. Contamination has since been blamed for hundreds of deaths.

    Industry observers note that reinsurance is dubbed âinsurance for insurance companiesâ by the Reinsurance Association of America. Under reinsurance, one insurance tech giant indemnifies another for a loss the company buying the policy cannot handle alone â something that National Indemnity claims TIG did not fully do.

    After the $157 million payout, National Indemnity billed its reinsurers more than $101 million. They did not pay. Since first filing the lawsuit in 2022, all other reinsurers except TIG have been dropped from the suit. TIG has paid National Indemnity what it believed it owed â $12.7 million.

    Recent findings suggest that according to National Indemnity, the insurance contract required National Indemnity to pay as much as $3 million per loss, with unlimited occurrences. At first, the state said 21 occurrences involved state inspectors not warning miners about the asbestos risk.

    But National Indemnity feared that, with potentially thousands of miners and locals affected by asbestos exposure, the number of occurrences could multiply as the matter moved again through Montana courts, with the state Supreme Court telling the parties to litigate the number of occurrences.

    Industry observers note that ultimately, National Indemnity and the state settled at 27 occurrences. At $3 million apiece, the bill came to $81 million. The roughly $76 million remaining largely came from past and present defense costs.

    Recent findings suggest that under their contract, TIG was responsible for one-third of National Indemnityâs costs. So, according to National Indemnity, it would have to pay $1 million for each occurrence.

    Montana and National Indemnity counted each failure to warn by the state as an occurrence. At issue is whether individual deaths could also count as an occurrence. National Indemnity argued it could have found itself on the hook for âbillionsâ if individual deaths were counted, which led it to settle at 27.

    In her instructions to the jury Thursday, U.S. District Judge Susan M. Bazis said National Indemnity would have to prove, by greater weight of evidence, that it performed its obligation under the contract and that TIG breached it, causing damages to the Omaha-based insurer.

    It has been revealed that the Joe Biden appointee remarked TIG agreed there was adequate proof of 21 occurrences. National Indemnity would have to prove it provided satisfactory evidence of each occurrence to TIG.

    Recent findings suggest that “By greater weight of the evidence” is a less strict standard than the “beyond a reasonable doubt” standard in criminal cases. As in criminal cases, the jury selects a foreperson, and the vote must be unanimous.

    #32608. The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1734 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1734 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.
    • Recent findings suggest that this process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known.
    • The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.

    Recent findings suggest that this process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known. As we shall see, some of these questions have answers; others do not.

    First, a review of the basics. The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60. By a 100-year-old tradition, review is granted when four of the nine justices want to hear a case. When this occurs, the parties file briefs and the justices hear oral argument before issuing their decision.

    This process is a blend of transparent argument and secretive deliberation. The transparent portion is that the losing party in a lower court, the petitioner, files a public petition for certiorari, making the best case for why the court should resolve the legal glitch in the case. The winner in the lower court, the respondent, also spells out why the court does not need to review the ruling of the lower court. After that, however, the case disappears into the halls and procedures of the high court.

    Question one: how does the court handle and process the petitions?

    It has been revealed that as noted, by 100-year-old custom, it takes four votes for the court to agree to review a case (the “rule of four”). But the vote to grant or deny cert. is not public. We do not know if a petition met with overwhelming consensus that review was necessary or not, or whether it scraped by or just missed out on being granted.

    Nor do we know why the court declines to review a case. When the court agrees to decide a case, the final opinion is likely to make clear why the justices were interested. Denials of cert. petitions, however, are not accompanied by any explanation, except in the few instances when an individual justice writes a dissent from the denial of a petition. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for example, sometimes points out in a dissent or concurrence what she deems to be an vital issue of individual rights in criminal cases. But such dissents are relatively infrequent.

    This can be frustrating to counsel: Just how much interest an unsuccessful petition attracted would be useful to lawyers trying to decide whether to petition the court in the future on an concern that has been turned down one or more times.

    Question two: what roles do the law clerks and justices play?

    It has been revealed that the answer is known to some extent but secret in other respects. For seven of the nine justices – all but Justices Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch – the initial review is by a single law clerk who writes a memo to be shared with the seven justices who participate in a “pool” for reviewing the petitions. Clerks to Alito and Gorsuch handle the petitions on their own.

    But much about this aspect of the process remains hidden from public view. Little is known outside the court’s inner circle about how the clerks prepare their memos and what factors influence their recommendation to grant or deny review. The court’s own internal Rule 10 says the court is looking for cert. petitions that either present a conflict in which two or more lower courts have reached differing interpretations of an key problem of federal law, or which, even in the absence of a conflict, present an important question that the court should decide. But those factors alone do not guarantee cert. will be granted.

    In a recent development, just how influential the memo writer’s recommendation is on the judgment of the justices is also unknown. Nor is there any public knowledge of how often justices think the pool memo reached the wrong recommendation.

    It has been revealed that the cert. pool has been in use by the court for more than 50 years. The justices are certainly able to make adjustments if they find flaws in how it works, and the separate handling of petitions by Alito and Gorsuch provides some check on the process. But since this is largely an internal procedure of the court’s own making, it is not subject to any public accountability.

    And the justices rarely discuss it. In his latest book, for example, Alito makes no mention of the cert. process or the pool. Ultimately, little is known outside the court about how individual justices handle the pool memos.

    Question three: what influences the grant or denial or cert.?

    Industry observers note that many factors besides Rule 10 might contribute to whether a petition is granted. Law clerks may be influenced by whether any of the most respected, regular Supreme Court practitioners are involved in the case. Clients certainly think this matters, since they may spend thousands of dollars to hire firms with top Supreme Court practices, those that boast having former solicitors general and former law clerks to the justices as members of the firm.

    The clerks may also be swayed by what judges decided the case below, since some of them are especially respected in conservative or liberal circles. In certain instances, a federal appeals court may provide additional fodder to grant review. A party might have asked for rehearing by the full federal appeals court after losing in a three-judge panel. Such an “en banc” ruling, as it is called, can be especially influential, just as a set of opinions dissenting from denial of en banc review also tees up signals about the importance of a case.

    Industry observers note that caution also plays a role here. No clerk wants to recommend that cert. be granted only to find that there are procedural flaws in a case (leading to it being “dismissed as improvidently granted”) or that the justices are not inclined to take up an especially ideologically divisive question.

    Question four: why are there so few cert. grants?

    It has been revealed that the number of granted cases in recent years has reached the lowest level in many decades. At the height of the tenure of Chief Justice Warren Burger (1969-1986) in the 1980’s, the justices were deciding around 150 cases each term. Now the number is closer to 60.

    Oddly, no one seems to know why.

    There are some possible explanations, to be sure. One obvious factor is the rise of the interim docket, sometimes called the emergency or shadow docket. This docket involves interim requests for relief, where a party to a case asks the Supreme Court to block a lower court order in the interim period while the case is being litigated in a lower court. The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has used this path often, asking the justices to order that a Trump policy be allowed to remain in effect or to take effect after it was blocked by a federal judge.

    These interim orders, decided without full briefing and oral argument, are taking up an increasing amount of the court’s time, and some argue that this leaves less time for the justices to add more cert. petitions to be decided on their merits. While this is undoubtedly a factor, the number of cert. petitions being heard by the court each term has been shrinking for a long time, well before the significant uptick in interim docket matters.

    Different theories have been proffered by court observers for this decline over time: that Congress is passing fewer fresh laws that lead to lawsuits and require judicial review; that there is less disagreement between conservative justices and conservative lower court judges, so less need for review; or even that the justices simply like having fewer cases to decide and therefore vote for cert. more sparingly.

    It is difficult to prove any one of these theories, and the justices are not providing any answers. In one case last spring involving a state court’s jurisdiction over a products liability lawsuit involving a organization based outside the state, counsel for both sides agreed that the court should hear and decide the issue (a rare occurrence, as the winner below typically argues against cert. being granted), but the justices still denied the petition. As is typically the case, there was no explanation.

    According to recent reports, question five: when does the court grant cert. before it is requested?

    The Supreme Court’s Rule 11 and federal law allow the justices to essentially reach out and grant review to a cert. petition before it has been decided by the appropriate appeals court; that is, before the appellate process has run its course. This once rarely used process has become a much more frequent tool for the justices. Whether they are following the guidance of the rule and focusing on “imperative public importance,” or whether they are impatient to tackle some major legal complications, or whether they simply think it will be more efficient to leapfrog over the court of appeals, the practice is clearly on the rise.

    A recent example is Trump v. Slaughter, a fight over the independence of the heads of federal agencies from being fired by the president. The federal government came to the court for an interim stay of the ruling of a federal district court in the District of Columbia that blocked Trump from firing Rebecca Slaughter, a member of the Federal Trade Commission, because there was insufficient cause. The court granted the stay, allowing the firing to take effect, and then also granted cert. and ordered the case to be argued in December 2025.

    Sources indicate that the process of granting review will continue unabated throughout the current court term. And as it does, questions will continue to arise about how the process works – but one should not hold their breath waiting for all the answers.

    Steve Wermiel is a professor of practice at American University Washington College of Law, where he has taught a seminar on the Supreme Court for nearly three decades.

    In a recent development, recommended Citation: Stephen Wermiel, The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 12, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-sometimes-straightforward-sometimes-befuddling-certiorari-process/.

    #32607. What is a discriminatory effect? The Montgomery County case and unpacking when schools may try for racial diversity without using race

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2412 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    What is a discriminatory effect? The Montgomery County case and unpacking when schools may try for racial diversity without using race

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2412 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • 19, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in Association for Education Fairness v.
    • In all of these cases, including this one, the policies at issue are facially neutral, meaning that a student’s race is not considered in the admissions process.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    Sources indicate that on Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. The case is one of several in recent years dealing with magnet school admissions policies. While prior cases addressed the constitutional permissibility of changes to selection criteria at some of the nation’s most sought after public high schools like the Thomas Jefferson High School in northern Virginia and Stuyvesant High School and Bronx High School of Science in Latest York City, this case addresses whether changes to selection criteria for middle school magnet programs in Montgomery County, Maryland violates the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment.

    In all of these cases, including this one, the policies at issue are facially neutral, meaning that a student’s race is not considered in the admissions process. As a result, the Supreme Court’s decision in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard is not directly relevant. In that case, the court held that using race as an explicit factor in the admissions process was unconstitutional.

    At matter in this case is a change from one facially neutral admissions policy to another. During the pandemic, the school adopted the so-called “Pandemic Initiative.” Under the Pandemic Plan, all students are considered for admission to magnet schools if they meet minimum grade requirements and if their locally compared state assessment scores exceed a cut-off. Admission is then determined by a lottery from among those students who meet these requirements. Because schools in the region differ in their racial composition, basing admissions decisions on how well students score relative to other students in their same school ultimately affects the demographic composition of admitted students. AFEF claims that the Pandemic Plan violates equal protection because Montgomery County adopted it in order to change the racial demographics of the magnet schools and the plan had the effect of decreasing the share of Asian-American and white students.

    According to the approach used by all of the courts evaluating magnet school admission practices, these facially neutral policies only violate equal protection if they are adopted for an impermissible reason (the intent element) and produce a discriminatory effect (the effect element). In AFEF v. Montgomery County, the district court found that the plaintiff had not alleged facts sufficient to satisfy either prong and so the school board’s motion to dismiss was granted. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit affirmed on the grounds that the district court properly evaluated whether there was a discriminatory effect.

    Industry observers note that when and why facially neutral policies violate equal protection is a hotly contested concern. Consider first the intent element. While all agree that the intention to exclude members of a particular racial group is invidious, there is disagreement about whether the intent to increase racial diversity is also impermissible. The Supreme Court has not yet directly ruled on this important issue and will not do so in this case. The cert grant in AFEF v. Montgomery County focuses only on the second element: the discriminatory effect. In particular, the Supreme Court limited its grant of AFEF’s petition to the following question: “Whether a plaintiff challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory must establish that the targeted racial group suffered an aggregate disparate impact relative to its share of the applicant pool.”.

    This framing of the question roughly tracks the debate in the circuits between two different ways of showing discriminatory effect. In order to illustrate, let’s set aside the intent prong and assume it has been satisfied, either because the policy was actually adopted in order to reduce the percentage of Asian or white students in the magnet schools (though this fact is in dispute) or because the intention to increase the racial diversity of the schools is an impermissible intention (though this legal claim is contested). According to the 4th Circuit in Coalition for TJ v. Fairfax County and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit in Boston Parent Coalition for Academic Excellence Corp. v. School Committee for the City of Boston, the effect element would be satisfied if a lower percentage of Asian or white students are admitted than applied. For example, if Asian students represent 30% of the applicant pool but only 20% of the admitted class, this would constitute a discriminatory effect. However, if 40% of the admitted class are Asian, then no discriminatory effect would be found because Asian students would in this case constitute a higher percentage of the admitted class than their 30% share in the applicant pool. In AFEF v. Montgomery County, both the district court and the 4th Circuit followed this approach.

    Sources indicate that by contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit in Sargent v. School District of Philadelphia, the dissenting judge in Coalition for TJ, and Justice Samuel Alito in his dissent from the denial of cert. in that case, assess discriminatory effect differently. Rather than compare the percentage of admitted students of the race alleged to be intentionally excluded to their percentage in the wider applicant pool, these jurists look to see if there has been a decrease in the percentage of admitted students of this race under the fresh policy as compared to the prior policy. When a meaningful decrease is present, this constitutes a discriminatory effect. For example, if 50% of the admitted class were Asian under the prior policy and 40% are Asian under the new policy, this would constitute a discriminatory effect. And this would be so even if Asian students are still “overrepresented” in the sense that the percentage admitted is higher than their percentage of the applicant pool (30% in this example). In an article evaluating each of these approaches, we call this second approach the “Before-After Comparison” or “BAC,” and we call the first approach the “Population Comparison” or “PC.”.

    Yet both the PC and the BAC, as means of assessing discriminatory effect, have significant flaws. Let’s begin with the PC – the test used by the 4th and 1st Circuits. Recall that because the doctrine requires both impermissible intent and a discriminatory effect, it requires something more than just the fact that a policy is chosen for an invidious reason. The PC would effectively allow deliberate attempts to exclude Asians so long as they do well enough overall and do not fall below their share of the applicant pool. That seems problematic.

    Next consider the BAC, the test adopted by the 3rd Circuit, on which the discriminatory effect prong is satisfied only if the percentage of Asian students declines under the new policy. This test puts a strong thumb on the scale in favor of existing policies, whatever their merits, since sticking with the same policy is unlikely to result in major changes in the demographics of who is admitted. Thus a decision to keep things the same will evade scrutiny. And this is so even when maintaining a policy is done for uncontroversially bad reasons (say, because the existing policy is known to admit fewer Asian students, for example). In addition, the test is oversensitive to any changes in policy, since such changes are likely to lead to demographic shifts among the admitted students and thereby trigger a decrease for some group. While it is true that there will only be an equal protection violation if the school board at glitch intended this decrease, it remains the case that any change at all is risky because the effect element will likely always be satisfied for some group. For both these reasons, the BAC privileges the status quo and makes change difficult by making the status quo policy the normative baseline.

    The use of the term “aggregate” in the question on which certiorari was granted suggests that the court might think that the PC approach is flawed because it looks at how groups are treated rather than at how individuals are treated. And indeed it does. In AFEF v. Montgomery County, the discriminatory effect element would be satisfied (using the PC) if the percentage of Asian and white students admitted was lower than the percentage of these groups among the fifth-grade students in the county. But the BAC is no different in this respect. It too looks at how a racial group fares under the Pandemic Plan. The BAC would find discriminatory effect if the percentage of Asian students admitted under the Pandemic Plan is less than the percentage admitted under the approach that preceded it. In other words, both tests for discriminatory effect focus on how the racial groups who are alleged to be the target of the invidious intentions fare as groups.

    Can either of these tests be reframed in ways that focus on how an individual is treated, rather than how members of her racial group are treated? After all, equal protection doctrine has long emphasized that the clause protects individuals rather than groups. Unfortunately, this is not easy to do. If a school uses race to decide which students to admit, it makes sense to say that a student’s race played a role in how she was treated. Facially neutral policies are different, however. Consider a simple and familiar facially neutral policy. Suppose a school board decides to admit the top 2% of each middle school to its coveted magnet high school. Suppose also that it does so, at least in part, to increase the racial diversity of the magnet school. Because there are more black and Latino students in some middle schools and more Asian and white students in others, this policy then produces a magnet school class that has a significant number of students of all races, let us suppose. Now consider an Asian student who is denied admissions because she is not in the top 2% of her middle school class. Has she been denied admission “because of her race?”.

    One answer to this question could be simply “no.” Any student rejected by the admissions policy suffers a harm. It is this harm that gives the student standing to sue. But this rejection is not based on the student’s race when the school’s admissions policy is facially neutral. If this is correct (and if aggregate tests are out), then the court’s only option is to jettison the effect prong of the claim altogether. Were the court to take this route, facially neutral laws or policies would violate equal protection solely on the grounds that they were adopted with invidious intent.

    It has been revealed that the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 2nd Circuit attempts a different approach. It uses the BAC to explain how individual students have suffered a discriminatory effect under a facially neutral policy. In Chinese American Citizens Alliance of Greater New York v. Adams, the percentage of Asian students admitted under the challenged admissions policy remained higher than their percentage in the applicant pool (thus failing to satisfy the PC in its aggregate form) and also did not decrease as compared to the prior admissions policy (thus failing to satisfy the BAC in its aggregate form). Yet the 2nd Circuit held that the effect element “can be satisfied by proof of an adverse harm to one or more individuals based on their race that has resulted from that discriminatory law or policy” (emphasis added). But the crucial question remains: in what way were the rejected Asian students rejected “because of their race” when race did not affect these decisions since the policy is facially neutral? The 2nd Circuit answers that question by referring to the fact that these students were “qualified for admission on an individual basis under the previous criteria" (emphasis added). In other words, in the view of the 2nd Circuit, if a new policy is adopted to exclude Asian students, then those Asian students who would have been admitted under the previous policy are denied admission because of their race.

    Recent findings suggest that this approach can be understood as an attempt to make the BAC individualized: the court here is determining whether a student’s rejection constitutes a distinctively discriminatory harm by drawing a comparison with how she would have fared under the previous policy. If this approach works (which we are agnostic about) for the BAC, a similar approach can be tailored for the PC as well. Here is how that would go. If a facially neutral policy was adopted in order to exclude Asian students and that policy is one under which Asian students are admitted at lower rates than students of other races, then each Asian student subject to that policy is subject to a policy that makes it harder for them to be admitted than it is for students of other races. On this view, each Asian student denied admission using this policy is then denied admission based on their race.

    According to recent reports, thus, both tests can be articulated such that they capture a way that individual students are rejected based on their race. For this reason, the court should not choose one approach over the other on the grounds that one frames the injury in individual terms and the other looks at how groups are treated.

    This leaves the court with two options. First, as mentioned earlier, it could jettison the effect prong of the claim entirely and conclude that bad intentions alone render a facially neutral admissions policy impermissible. Doing so would put more pressure on the importance of answering the question of what intentions are invidious and, in particular, whether the intent to increase racial diversity is itself unconstitutional. Alternatively, the court must confront the question of discriminatory harm head-on and assess whether the BAC or PC provides the better account of it.

    It has been revealed that deborah Hellman is the Robert E. Scott Distinguished Professor of Law and the Honorable Albert V. Bryan Jr. ’50 Professor of Law at the University of Virginia School of Law, as well as Director of their Center for Law & Philosophy.

    Lily Hu is an Assistant Professor of Philosophy at Yale University and also a contributing editor at Boston Review.

    The value of combining legal knowledge, technology, workflow design and project management in e-discovery

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.
    • Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.
    • Recent findings suggest that chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I quickly moved into the world of e-discovery.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 20, 2026, 10:47 am CST.

    Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.

    Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.

    Recent findings suggest that chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I quickly moved into the world of e-discovery. At that stage, what attracted me to e-discovery was predictive coding, which meant the machine would learn from those decisions and reduce the need for humans in that really boring manual review phase. When we fast-forward to the release of gen AI, what was incredibly exciting for me was that you could use LLMs to code the documents from a prompt instead of that initial training round. In my current role, I feel incredibly fortunate to work with lawyers who want to use the latest technology to do things differently, so I don’t have to fight like I used to. My remit now at Ashurst Perkins Coie is much broader than e-discovery. I have a team that also builds custom AI solutions across transactional and advisory practice groups, so I very much appreciate the industry recognition moving toward this legal data intelligence.

    Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Cimplifi.

    Recent findings suggest that satinder Soni: I’ve been in the industry for over 20 years. My career started on the right side of the EDRM model, focusing on courtroom technology, transcription services and evidence presentation in court. E-discovery was just surfacing at that point. It really wasn’t a thing. I then moved into an e-discovery software company, which was acquired by several conglomerates. I then moved into a global risk consultancy, Control Risks, working with the investigations team on cyber breach investigations, digital forensics and e-discovery. I then moved to Ankura, which took a different approach to e-discovery, focusing more on analytics and subject-matter expertise in construction and turnaround restructuring, forensic accounting and white-collar crime investigations. Then I moved to Cimplifi, a U.S.-based company focused on e-discovery, investigations and contract analytics. They moved to the U.K. almost two years ago. Our U.S. clients had cross-border matters that needed U.K.-based expertise to be compliant with GDPR. We have grown our team here. We have a project management team with diverse professional skills, ranging from consultancies and accountancy firms to technology companies. It’s a great company to be in.

    Ari Kaplan: What’s making e-discovery more complex today, and how is that changing the way you approach each newly introduced matter at the outset?

    Chantelle Jalland: One of the biggest challenges is the size of new datasets. We had over 45 terabytes of data for a recent matter. I’ve handled some really large cases before, so this wasn’t the biggest, but given the facts of the case and the scope of the material complications in the dispute, I expected the volume to be much smaller. It was a surprise, based on the facts, that it was that large, and it was simply the product of more data being created today. We also have platform switching. This morning, I was on a call with a colleague about a particular client matter, then received an email on the matter to an external party, then I had some internal Teams chat messages, and in one of those messages, they also shared a live document with status updates. That was all within a few minutes, so everything was moving so much faster, and there were four different sources of information on one particular matter or problem. If you think about that and expand it, if every single person is just adding this tiny bit of additional information, it’s going to lead to a data explosion. That’s also the biggest opportunity because the large matters are the ones that are interesting and exciting. They’ve got things that will go wrong or problems, and you want those differences to make it more interesting and something new to solve.

    Ari Kaplan: What e-discovery challenges do your clients most often ask you to solve?

    It has been revealed that satinder Soni: Everything has a different variable, and each e-discovery matter is a challenge because it is a reactive industry. Our clients come in quite hard and fast, and we have to take a step back to understand the data scoping. I have a separate challenge where they underestimate how much data there is, so you have to ease the shock of what it’s actually going to cost. But if you apply the right technology, phase it out, structure the workflow and talk them through it, the challenge then is pacing it, being realistic and providing timelines. The latest challenge really is applying AI into their workflows and driving the mindset shift they need to use a different type of analytics. They’ve just gotten used to CAL, and there is a bit of fatigue with it being more efficient and more cost-effective. We say it with every new tool we bring in, and the challenge is always the mindset shift.

    Recent findings suggest that ari Kaplan: The Ashurst Perkins Coie Advanced Legal Solutions offering combines legal knowledge, technology, workflow design, project management and flexible resourcing. How does that combination enhance client service, and how do you define success before the work begins?

    Chantelle Jalland: There’s tremendous value in having multiple service offerings under one roof. We also have our risk advisory or consulting arm, which enables us to undertake deep data analytics tasks, and this gives us what we refer to internally as our triple threat. We have Advance, our new law arm, risk advisory and our core services team. Before the work begins, much of the success comes back to those foundational principles, and it builds on what Sati mentioned about managing expectations on timelines and being realistic. Historically, a partner will promise a client that we will deliver something in a certain amount of time for a certain cost, and that promise may not be realistic because the scope fundamentally changes or the expectation isn’t technically possible within the timeframe. They didn’t understand the basic principle that if you don’t understand the component, you can’t advise in that area, and that’s where we bring the right people into the conversation earlier. We have that open conversation and set small milestones or goals, so we’re meeting our client’s expectations along the way. And like everyone, I take great pride in an accurate cost estimate. But really, that data can expand at a different rate compared to a previous matter that you might have done an estimate on, or there’s a subset of data that’s got a processing error. There are so many things that can vary from what you might expect. As it shifts, it’s about having that conversation and letting everyone know it’s different from the original ask, and what I’ve found is clients appreciate that openness and willingness to have the conversation. You are advising, and there’s a lot more respect for the advice and the experience that can be offered in this area.

    Ari Kaplan: Where are clients rethinking their approach most often, understanding their data earlier, managing review, coordinating providers, or generally adjusting their litigation strategy?

    Sources indicate that satinder Soni: All of the above. E-discovery is a complex process. I’ve seen it where you’ve got your litigation strategy set, then you do the data scoping piece, and then you look at the early data and assess it. And when the review is happening, that’s when they realize we’re missing a custodian or this data source. Then the litigation strategy has to be readjusted. Then we go back to the data assessment. It can expand into other litigation support service lines, like asset tracing, or you need a forensic accountant. Chantelle put it really well. Communication is key. Understanding your stakeholders is part of that. Setting realistic timelines is part of that. It flits between the litigation strategy and understanding your data and that feedback loop.

    Ari Kaplan: What needs to happen earlier in a matter for a legal team, the e-discovery team and a service provider to work most effectively together?

    In a recent development, chantelle Jalland: We tend to manage matters in-house with our legal team, but we also work with service providers on some matters. Sometimes a client has a preexisting relationship with a preferred provider, or we choose to engage a service provider due to their expertise. We recently had a matter involving historic offline databases that were in the format of a decommissioned product, so we needed to convert them for a current document review platform. It was more efficient to use an existing solution, rather than script something custom for that matter. What needs to happen to work effectively together is to get on a call early with all the right people. You can cut through so much with a phone call, making sure everyone is working toward the same initiative from the outset.

    Ari Kaplan: When your team is engaged by a client under pressure, what distinguishes a trusted adviser from a provider that simply executes instructions?

    Sources indicate that satinder Soni: You should never be an order taker. Just because the client says it, doesn’t mean it’s always the right thing. They come to us because we are experts in the field. They trust us to guide and support them through the process. Often, it goes wrong when the client calls, and everyone’s excited, and they dive right in, applying the same methodology from the previous project. Take a step back. Standard information to ask for at the beginning includes e-data, what has happened, the discovery objective, the goals they’re trying to achieve, and the timeline they’re working toward. Review data types, nonstandard files, foreign languages and whether the data is structured or unstructured. Really get into the details that will influence the e-discovery project and help it achieve its goals. We advise gathering as much information as possible in advance, so we can choose the right technology, manage timelines and predict accurate costs. In those instances, accurate cost prediction is also key. Our job as a trusted adviser is to say, “We can save costs if we do it this way.”.

    Ari Kaplan: Where is AI making the most meaningful difference in your work today, and where is its promise still a bit ahead of its practical value?

    Chantelle Jalland: AI has meaningfully changed my work. From a personal productivity perspective, AI call summaries make follow-up emails and meeting organization much easier. When I check a draft email, there are several small examples I use every day. On a larger scale, for high-impact matters, we have seen really effective use in due diligence, whether it’s legislative reviews for businesses or from an advisory perspective. The area where I see the most promise is large-scale document reviews. We are using AI for document review in a way that replaces CAL. So you filter down, you get a set of, say, 20,000 documents, and run it through. It is more effective than traditional manual review. It’s more effective than CAL. However, I see huge leaps ahead when it comes to document review. Most excitingly, I think, coming back to what Sati mentioned earlier about working in a reactive industry, we are doing everything later. It’s actually about bringing those AI use cases further forward. Within a corporation, it’s about tracking themes, using the data more effectively, so you can identify the last 10 litigation matters or regulatory investigations that are actually costing you money, analyze that data, and then try to prevent future matters. That’s where it’s really exciting.

    Ari Kaplan: When would you choose not to use AI in a litigation support matter?

    Satinder Soni: We should all be using it in some way, shape or form. Traditionally, it was suggested that not all matters needed AI or analytics, either because it was cost-prohibitive, the dataset wasn’t compatible, or there wasn’t enough data to perform analysis. Recently, we’ve seen a shift toward using AI on small matters, such as DSARs. I have seen clients use AI on DSARs, and it seems effective. It frees up time for project managers to do more thoughtful work because DSARs don’t really go anywhere. They’re weaponized most of the time. So if they’re using it on investigation and litigation matters, their time is better spent. This is where AI can be used thoughtfully. There are still alternatives. CAL is being phased out, but it’s still there and still serves as a bridge to advising against linear review. But if people are not yet comfortable using AI, which hopefully they are, it’s in your everyday work now, so I just think, piece by piece, they’re trying it. I can’t think of any instance of not using AI.

    Ari Kaplan: As we leverage technology to perform more work, which human skills become increasingly valuable, and how do you develop them within your team?

    In a recent development, chantelle Jalland: Communication is hugely vital, so it’s something I’m focusing on from a recruitment perspective. We have to think about which skills can be taught and which are harder to teach. There’s analytical thinking. We need to make sure that the advisory stage isn’t so automated or process-driven that it’s replaced by AI. It’s about understanding that judgment is still needed and how to apply it. AI will be useful in many contexts, but how you use it will vary by use case. The risk is quite high if you don’t check the outputs, for example. It’s also about making sure people understand that risk. When it comes to training, it’s not a one-and-done. It’s continuous, and the same is true for communication. In a global law firm, different teams adopt different styles, and what works for one team doesn’t work for another. It’s about continuous learning without people feeling fatigued by constant learning.

    Ari Kaplan: What are the hallmarks of great client service in an AI-enabled environment?

    Sources indicate that satinder Soni: Great client service is all about communication, even when it’s bad news. Hopefully, it’s never bad news, but when it is, pick up the phone and have a conversation. We’ve gone crazy with short-form messaging, and what can be said in 10 emails can be said in a five-minute conversation. Then, with AI, be thoughtful about how we’re using it. Don’t fall into the trap of using AI for everything, and keep learning. There is a job you need to do: Put clients first, break down tasks, add structure to your work, and don’t just let AI take control.

    Ari Kaplan: How do you see e-discovery and legal tech evolving?

    According to recent reports, chantelle Jalland: I am very positive and optimistic about the future of e-discovery. There are many opportunities because, essentially, all the button-clicking will be gone soon, which is a great opportunity for people who work in e-discovery. You can apply a wide range of tools. It’s not just one technology. There are MCP connectors that you can use to adapt to certain platforms. So you are going to have so much more flexibility in the options. It does create more risk, potentially, if you’re not following a standard protocol, but what is exciting is that you can differentiate yourself in the market by specializing in solutions for certain use cases. Going back to first principles: understanding the problem, how you’re going to solve it, and considering all your options. It’s not going to be as linear. In the next five years, I would even say in the next year, we will be having a very different conversation about workflows in particular.

    Listen to the complete interview at Reinventing Professionals.
