    #32475. Google Ads AI Max Is Making More Decisions For You – 6 Settings To Audit Now via @sejournal, @brookeosmundson

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1708 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Google Ads AI Max Is Making More Decisions For You – 6 Settings To Audit Now via @sejournal, @brookeosmundson

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google Ads is moving more existing Search campaign functionality into AI Max, giving its automation a larger role in how ads are matched, written, and delivered.
    • Campaigns using automatically created assets and campaign-level broad match settings already began transitioning in September 2026.
    • It has been revealed that google says the automatic upgrades are designed to preserve existing campaign settings.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google Ads is moving more existing Search campaign functionality into AI Max, giving its automation a larger role in how ads are matched, written, and delivered.

    Campaigns using automatically created assets and campaign-level broad match settings already began transitioning in September 2026. Dynamic Search Ads will follow in February 2027.

    It has been revealed that google says the automatic upgrades are designed to preserve existing campaign settings. However, AI Max also brings additional controls and optimization options that advertisers have the option to enable.

    For PPC managers, this is a good time to review which decisions Google is already making, which settings are active in your accounts, and whether those settings are aligned with your business goals.

    Here’s what to audit before giving AI Max more control over existing Search campaigns.

    Before changing anything, it’s crucial to understand how AI Max is currently configured across your accounts, if at all.

    Google’s migration process doesn’t enable every AI Max feature automatically for every campaign. The settings depend on which legacy functionality each campaign was using.

    According to Google’s migration documentation:.

    This is why it’s worth checking each campaign, because two campaigns showing AI Max as enabled may have very different levels of automation running.

    In a recent development, within Google Ads, review the AI Max settings at both the campaign and ad group levels. Specifically, check whether search term matching, text customization, and Final URL expansion are active.

    Search term matching can be controlled at the ad group level, while text customization and Final URL expansion are campaign-level settings.

    I’d also look at whether any campaigns have different configurations than expected, especially those that were recently migrated or created using Google’s default settings.

    The goal here is to establish what’s running before making additional changes. Otherwise, it becomes difficult to evaluate which AI Max features are influencing performance.

    Search term matching is one of the areas I’d spend the most time reviewing, especially in campaigns with tightly defined keyword strategies.

    AI Max can use broad match and keywordless matching technology to identify additional searches based on existing keywords, ads, and landing pages.

    While it can help campaigns reach relevant searches that weren’t covered by the original keyword list, it’s also notorious for introducing traffic that doesn’t fit the campaign’s intended purpose.

    Research from Mike Ryan at Smarter Ecommerce (SMEC) shows how much AI Max can expand beyond an advertiser’s existing keyword targeting.

    In an analysis of 383 million impressions, Ryan found that more than 25% of impressions attributed to exact match keywords in AI Max-enabled Search campaigns came through AI Max search term matching.

    That doesn’t mean those searches were necessarily irrelevant. However, it does show why advertisers shouldn’t assume exact match keywords are limiting traffic to their original targeting.

    Google’s AI Max reporting documentation outlines additional reporting fields that can help advertisers understand how searches are being matched.

    When reviewing Search terms, I’d focus on:.

    Competitor searches might deserve some extra attention, based on Ryan’s research.

    In SMEC’s research, Ryan documented one account where competitor searches accounted for 69% of total Search impressions.

    That’s a single-account example, but it reveals how heavily the traffic mix can lean toward searches outside the advertiser’s original targeting.

    I also wouldn’t judge every new search term solely by whether it converts immediately.

    Some campaigns may have some wiggle room to support earlier-stage research, especially when there’s enough budget to fund it without taking away from stronger existing demand.

    However, if a campaign is already struggling to capture its highest-intent searches, expanding into more informational traffic might be worth excluding for the time being.

    Negative keywords remain available with AI Max, along with brand controls and ad group-level locations of interest.

    Text customization allows Google to generate additional headlines and descriptions using existing ads, keywords, and landing page content.

    For advertisers already using automatically created assets, the audit should focus on what’s being generated and how those assets are performing.

    Google’s optimized asset reporting provides additional performance metrics, including spend and conversions, to help advertisers evaluate the assets being served.

    I’d look closely at three areas:.

    A generated headline could be technically accurate for the business but inappropriate for the campaign’s audience.

    This deserves additional review in industries with legal, compliance, or partner messaging requirements.

    Google allows advertisers to review and remove generated assets. It has also introduced AI Brief and text disclaimer controls to provide additional guidance over generated messaging.

    According to recent reports, see also: Should You Use Auto-Generated Creative? – Ask A PPC.

    There’s another consideration for campaigns that rely on responsive search ad pinning.

    Google’s AI Max documentation confirms that pinning isn’t always respected when Final URL expansion is enabled.

    Industry observers note that when Google selects a different landing page, it may generate ad copy that better matches that destination rather than using the advertiser’s pinned assets. Pinning also isn’t respected when URL inclusions are provided.

    For campaigns with required disclaimers, pricing language, or partner-approved messaging, I’d check whether the current settings support those requirements.

    If pinning is essential, Google recommends avoiding Final URL expansion and URL inclusions.

    When Final URL expansion is enabled, Google can select a different landing page from the advertiser’s website based on the search query.

    That may help when a website has several relevant product or service pages, but it can also create problems when the destination doesn’t align with the campaign’s goals.

    A website might contain informational articles, support documentation, and pages promoting services outside the campaign’s intended focus.

    Those pages could be relevant to someone’s search, but not something worth spending PPC dollars on.

    Google’s landing page and search term reporting can help identify which URLs are receiving traffic through AI Max.

    For lead generation, I’d also look beyond the initial form submission.

    It has been revealed that A landing page might generate more leads while attracting more unqualified customers. That can be difficult to identify without qualified lead or sales data.

    Google supports URL exclusions at the campaign level and URL inclusions at the ad group level.

    Those controls can help advertisers limit where traffic goes without necessarily turning off Final URL expansion across an entire campaign.

    For accounts with tightly controlled conversion experiences, I’d review the available URLs before enabling broader expansion.

    See also: Should Your PPC Strategy Focus On The Lead Pipeline Or Revenue?

    Google has reported that advertisers using the full AI Max feature suite see an average of 7% more conversions or conversion value at a similar CPA or ROAS compared with using search term matching alone.

    That figure comes from Google’s internal 2026 data for non-retail advertisers, and it shouldn’t be treated as an expected result for every account.

    Independent research from Smarter Ecommerce offers another perspective.

    In a March 2026 analysis of more than 250 campaigns, Mike Ryan found that AI Max generated a median 13% more conversion value relative to the remaining campaign revenue.

    However, those conversions came at a median CPA that was 16% higher than the campaign baseline.

    Recent findings suggest that ROAS results also varied considerably. While the median difference was 0%, individual campaign results ranged from 42% above baseline to 35% below it.

    These figures come from observational campaign data rather than controlled experiments measuring incremental performance. Ryan also noted that the analysis couldn’t account for potential cannibalization across campaigns.

    Sources indicate that the research doesn’t mean AI Max is underperforming across the board. It suggests that additional conversion volume may come at a higher cost, with results varying significantly between accounts.

    According to recent reports, if broader matching is reaching more informational or earlier-stage searches, those owners may need more time before converting. Some may never become customers.

    Sources indicate that for lead generation, I’d compare the quality of conversions coming through AI Max against existing traffic. Are those leads qualified? Are they turning into opportunities or customers?

    For ecommerce, revenue, ROAS, margin, and the products being sold can provide more information than conversion volume alone.

    Google has expanded its AI Max experimentation tools, including the ability to maintain brand and location controls during testing.

    For campaigns that haven’t fully adopted AI Max, experiments can help compare performance before enabling additional functionality.

    I’d avoid changing several settings at once because it’s more difficult to attribute performance swings to a particular feature set of AI Max.

    According to recent reports, if the goal is to understand whether broader matching improves performance, structure the test around that decision. The same applies to Final URL expansion or text customization.

    Google’s experiment setup has eligibility restrictions, so not every existing campaign can use the same testing approach.

    For campaigns already migrated with legacy functionality enabled, reviewing current performance may help identify which settings are worth testing next.

    Advertisers still running Dynamic Search Ads have time before Google’s automatic migration begins in February 2027.

    Google notes the migration will convert dynamic ad groups into standard ad groups while preserving supported legacy settings and data. Its upgrade documentation also notes that unsupported legacy DSA targets may become read-only.

    I’d review existing dynamic ad targets, URL exclusions, and search term performance before the transition.

    Some campaigns may contain targeting decisions that made sense when they were created but haven’t been revisited recently.

    For advertisers with complex websites or large inventories, confirming which pages and services should remain eligible is worth doing before the migration.

    I wouldn’t approach this audit by immediately turning off AI Max features or adding restrictions across every Search campaign.

    Some accounts may benefit from giving Google more flexibility to find relevant searches, customize messaging, and select landing pages.

    I’d start with campaigns where those decisions could have the greatest impact on performance or where existing controls serve a clear purpose.

    That includes campaigns with limited budgets, strict lead qualification requirements, regulated messaging, or carefully managed landing page experiences.

    For campaigns already performing well, reviewing current settings and reporting may be enough to determine whether additional testing is worthwhile.

    It has been revealed that as Google moves more Search functionality into AI Max, advertisers still have control over several important decisions. Knowing what’s enabled, how Google is using that flexibility, and what results the business is receiving should guide where those controls are applied.

    “I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, ‘OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.’”.

    It has been revealed that the data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

    For Nikita Redkar, a massive part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

    In a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around Newly introduced York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

    According to recent reports, in another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

    A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

    “I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar remarked. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”.

    In a recent development, redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

    Hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I said there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

But when I talk to my audience, I intentionally give them hope. I don’t just tell the news, but tell them, OK, if we really locked in and held these corporations and the government accountable and we were intentional in our activism, this is what the world could look like. I would like to think that someone who looks like me and talks like me should be just as interested in politics and just as interested in the outcome of this country.

    It has been revealed that redkar: On Mondays, I have a researcher and we go through the topics that people are talking about on social media. We pull up some news sites and see what the substantial stories are, and we leave some room for breaking news throughout the week.

    My week is [split] between videos [on topics] that the general public is talking about, and videos that are just interesting to me. That’s how I stay sane in this business.     Redkar: It’s definitely my favorite color, but it’s like the chicken and the egg — I don’t know if I liked it before I was doing this.

    Sources indicate that I pick whatever outfit I feel cute in. In getting ready with me videos, I start with a completely bare face, so at least the outfit has to be giving a little bit.

    It has been revealed that redkar: It’s like: What am I comfortable screaming out in the streets versus what do I need to keep at home?     Redkar: If I get a fact wrong, I’ll do a follow-up video. It’s rare that I’ve gotten a fact wrong because between me and my researcher, that’s two levels of checks before something hits the internet.

    Tech Report: Rank Math SEO WordPress Plugin Hit By 16 Vulnerabilities In 2026 via @sejournal, @martinibuster

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sixteen vulnerabilities have been discovered in the popular Rank Math SEO plugin in 2026, setting a new record for vulnerabilities discovered, more than any other SEO plugin.
    • Sources indicate that rank Math’s 2026 vulnerabilities included potential pathways to website takeover, exposure of protected information, and unauthorized changes to WordPress content and data.
    • Industry observers note that although AI is making vulnerability disclosures more common, other SEO plugins like Yoast SEO did not have anywhere near that many vulnerability discoveries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sixteen vulnerabilities have been discovered in the popular Rank Math SEO plugin in 2026, setting a new record for vulnerabilities discovered, more than any other SEO plugin.

    Sources indicate that rank Math’s 2026 vulnerabilities included potential pathways to website takeover, exposure of protected information, and unauthorized changes to WordPress content and data. All of these things could also have a negative impact on SEO.

    Industry observers note that although AI is making vulnerability disclosures more common, other SEO plugins like Yoast SEO did not have anywhere near that many vulnerability discoveries. The free version of Yoast SEO was reported by Wordfence to have a total of four vulnerabilities in 2026 and only two were discovered in the paid version.

    The sixteen vulnerabilities share certain complications in common but arguably the worst of them are:.

    Remote Code Execution (CVSS rated 8.8) Two vulnerabilities with a CVSS severity score of 8.8 were discovered that could enable attackers with Contributor or Author-level access to execute arbitrary code on the server, potentially leading to complete website compromise.

    Arbitrary File Upload (7.2) One of the vulnerabilities could potentially lead to a website takeover through malicious file uploads, although this vulnerability required Administrator privileges. CVE-2026-104752: Arbitrary File Upload, requiring Administrator-level access or higher. Disclosed October 8, 2026. CVSS 7.2 (High).

    Stored Cross-Site Scripting (7.2) An unauthenticated attacker could potentially execute malicious JavaScript in an Administrator’s browser. Depending on the circumstances, that could lead to privileged actions or account compromise. CVE-2026-66702: Stored Cross-Site Scripting, requiring no authentication. Disclosed July 31, 2026. CVSS 7.2 (High).

    Industry observers note that stored Cross-Site Scripting (7.2) An unauthenticated attacker could potentially execute malicious JavaScript in an Administrator’s browser. Depending on the circumstances, this could enable an attacker to make unauthorized changes to the website or take control of an Administrator’s account. CVE-2026-66702: Stored Cross-Site Scripting, requiring no authentication. Disclosed July 31, 2026. CVSS 7.2 (High).

    These vulnerabilities could allow attackers to access protected content or sensitive website information without the necessary permissions. Unlike vulnerabilities that enable unauthorized changes, these primarily concern exposing information that should remain restricted, although SQL injection could also allow attackers to manipulate website data.

    It has been revealed that these vulnerabilities could enable attackers to make unauthorized changes to a WordPress website, including modifying content-related data, changing homepage settings, and deleting SEO information. Some could be exploited without logging in, while others required an account but allowed actions beyond that user level’s permissions.

    Sources indicate that most vulnerabilities were discovered within a relatively short period. Eleven of the 16 vulnerabilities were discovered between August 27 and October 14, 2026. Of those vulnerabilities, late August and early September saw a concentrated cluster of vulnerability discoveries. Eight were reported between August 27 and September 3, within just eight days.

    In a recent development, the disclosures continued into October. Five vulnerabilities were reported in October, including three disclosed on October 8 and the latest on October 27.

    Industry observers note that as previously stated, Rank Math’s direct competitor, Yoast SEO, only experienced four vulnerabilities during a year which saw an increase in vulnerability discoveries. The unusually high number of vulnerabilities leads to questions about Rank Math’s coding practices, code review, and quality control.

    The other issue in the sixteen vulnerabilities is that are repeated instances of the same kinds of exploits.

    Missing authorization was the most frequently identified vulnerability category. Seven of the 16 entries explicitly mention inadequate permission checks, pointing to recurring problems with enforcing permissions before allowing actions.

    Industry observers note that some security problems could lead to complete website compromise. Two vulnerabilities carried CVSS scores of 8.8 and involved remote code execution, allowing attackers who met the required conditions to potentially execute malicious code on the server.

    In a recent development, overall, the vulnerabilities involved a broad range of security weaknesses. They included unauthorized modifications, information exposure, cross-site scripting, SQL injection, arbitrary file uploads, and remote code execution. The vulnerability discoveries do not point to just one type of coding lapse; they point to a wide range of coding issues.

    The full list of Rank Math vulnerabilities can be found at Wordfence, with links to a description page for each vulnerability.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Carnival Cruise Line aims to introduce a newly introduced class of ships to its fleet. Two LNG-powered ships of approximately 130,000 gross tons each will be built by Fincantieri for delivery in 2033 and 2035, according to a press release.

    Sources indicate that the organization noted the latest ships were intentionally designed on a smaller scale. That will give them access to more ports and widen the brand’s destination and itinerary options.

    “With a 29-ship fleet, we know our guests appreciate choices,” remarked Christine Duffy, president of Carnival Cruise Line.

    Recent findings suggest that “They love the incredible experiences and amenities on our Excel Class ships, the largest in our fleet, but they also love the intimacy our smaller ships offer. This newly introduced class gives us the best of both worlds, helping future-proof our fleet with the flexibility to take America’s Cruise Line to even more places in the years ahead.”.

    At the New York event on Thursday, Duffy also gave a first look at the upcoming Carnival Destiny. She outlined expansions at Celebration Key and RelaxAway, Half Moon Cay, and announced intends to extend popular onboard benefits ashore.

    Industry observers note that the Carnival Destiny will debut in 2029 as the first of three Ace Class ships. It will have more outdoor pools than any other Carnival ship: eight in total, including six infinity pools, with more than 11,200 square feet of water surface.     “We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.”.

    Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the company to scrape the websites of Meta Business account customers.

    On Thursday, the firm took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an update to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”.

    Meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20.

    Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting new commercial terms into effect.

    Industry observers note that “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms patch. We care deeply about our partners and do not strategy to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”.

    Sources indicate that since then, courts in Norway and Brazil have issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms from taking effect as a result of lawsuits filed by media organizations in both countries. The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into Meta, examining whether the firm was “abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers.”.

    Industry observers note that in the United States, the proposed terms stoked bipartisan concern. At the end of October, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking him to withdraw the terms.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    AI is changing how customers discover and evaluate brands.

    Enterprises need to think beyond rich results and develop the business context they publish for machines.

    In 2027, schema markup has to be upgraded in order to maintain visibility in AI SERPs.

    Get a free, personalized AI-Ready Schema Markup Scorecard, Now →.

    Sources indicate that the upcoming job I see for schema markup is to help AI understand your business, not just make individual pages eligible for rich results. That means explicitly describing your products, services, people, and locations, showing how they connect, and keeping those facts and relationships accurate as your business changes.

    Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest questions I hear from enterprise marketing leaders today is: How do we make sure AI is getting our brand right? It’s a fair question.

    In a recent development, AI is increasingly influencing how customers discover, research, and choose businesses. Unlike traditional search, where customers could visit your website and form their own understanding, AI now brings information together from across the web to create answers on their behalf.

    That information might come from your website, a third-party directory, customer reviews, or an article published years ago. And not all of it is necessarily accurate, complete, or up to date.

    Industry observers note that here’s what I think is key for marketers to recognize: You can’t control everything AI indicates about your business. But you can take greater control of the information you give it, and that starts with your website.

    Your website is one of the most valuable sources of information you own. It’s where you define who you are, what you offer, the expertise you bring to market, and what you want your business to be known for.

    This is why I believe preparing the information you own for AI is one of the most notable investments enterprise marketers can make today.

    And if your organization already has schema markup, you’ve already started building that foundation. The opportunity now is to think bigger about what it can do, and make sure your strategy is built for the job schema markup needs to do today and tomorrow, not just the one it did yesterday.

    Industry observers note that the good news is that if you’ve already invested in schema markup, you’re not starting from scratch. But not all schema markup is created equal. Before you focus on doing more, ask whether what you already have gives machines a clear, connected understanding of your business.

    The opportunity is to assess the foundation you’ve built, identify where it could be stronger, and build from there.

    Here are three questions I’d encourage enterprise marketing leaders to ask.

    Pro Tip: Use a AI-Ready Schema Markup Scorecard to assess your current foundation and identify opportunities to strengthen how machines understand your business.

    Having schema markup across your website is a great start. But is it capturing the information that actually matters to your business?

    Sources indicate that think about your most crucial products, services, locations, and areas of expertise. Does your markup describe them accurately and in enough detail? Or is it simply meeting the minimum requirements for a search feature? The goal isn’t just more schema markup; it’s more meaningful markup.

    Industry observers note that it’s one thing for machines to recognize the individual parts of your business. It’s another for them to understand how everything fits together. Are your people, products, services, and locations consistently identified and connected? Can machines recognize when different pages are talking about the same thing?

    Think about a healthcare system. It might have schema markup describing its physicians, hospitals, and medical services. That’s a great start. But does that information clearly communicate which physicians specialize in which treatments? Where they practice? Which services are available at each location? And how all of those things connect back to the healthcare system?

    Move beyond describing individual pages to communicating a connected picture of your business.

    Recent findings suggest that your business is constantly evolving. New services, new locations, new expertise. And as your website content changes, your schema markup needs to keep up. Because it’s not enough for your website to tell one story to customers while your structured data tells another to machines.

    As your website evolves, does your schema markup keep pace, reflecting the same accurate information and maintaining the relationships that connect your business?

    Industry observers note that our Wells Fargo case study illustrates why this matters. Wells Fargo encountered an AI Overview that incorrectly identified a branch as permanently closed. By strengthening the structured information on its website, the team helped address that inaccurate answer.

    In a recent development, you can’t control every answer AI generates. But you can take greater control of the accuracy and consistency of the information you’re giving it to work with. And that requires governance to be part of your approach from the beginning.

    We need to think differently about what we’re asking our schema markup to accomplish. We should question whether we’re giving machines the information and context they need to understand our business as a whole, and recognize our relevance to the topics that matter most.

    But here’s the challenge: Across large enterprise websites, that information is often spread across thousands of pages, managed by different teams, and constantly changing. Even when the information is accurate on individual pages, it doesn’t always tell a clear, connected story about the business.

    Industry observers note that and sometimes, we’re contributing to the confusion ourselves. As Schema App’s CTO Mark van Berkel discusses in Forbes, AI doesn’t always need to hallucinate incorrect information. Sometimes, it works with conflicting information businesses have already published.

    Sources indicate that if we want AI to understand our business, we need to give it more than individual pieces of information. We need to help it understand how those pieces fit together. And for large enterprises, that’s not a small challenge.

    It has been revealed that think about everything your organization publishes across its website. Your products and services, locations, your people and their expertise, the topics you want to be known for. All of that information helps tell the story of your business. But across thousands of pages, different teams, and constantly changing content, those connections aren’t always clear.

    Recent findings suggest that what if we started thinking about our website not just as a collection of pages, but as a connected source of truth about our business? That’s the opportunity I see with a Marketing Context Layer.

    A Marketing Context Layer is a governed foundation of information about your business that helps machines understand who you are, what you offer, what you’re known for, and how it all connects. It starts with the information you own and publish on your website.

    Through advanced schema markup, you can make important business facts and relationships explicit, connecting them into a Content Knowledge Graph that can be maintained as your business evolves.

    Sources indicate that and this isn’t just a marketing conversation. Forrester has been exploring the importance of context layers in enterprise AI, recognizing the role of connected business knowledge in helping AI systems interpret and use information. I believe there’s an important opportunity to apply that same thinking to marketing. If enterprises are investing in governed business context to power AI internally, shouldn’t we also be thinking about the context we’re publishing for AI to understand us externally?

    Sources indicate that this is where schema markup becomes much more than an SEO tactic. It’s the starting point for building a connected, governed foundation of information about your business. One you can keep improving, maintaining, and putting to work as search and AI experiences evolve.

    As our CTO, Mark van Berkel, explores in Forbes, the organizations that want to make meaningful use of AI need to invest in the information foundations that support it.

    Recent findings suggest that I believe we’re at an exciting turning point for enterprise marketers. We’ve spent years investing in our websites, creating content, and building our presence in search. Now we have an opportunity to make those investments work harder by helping machines understand the business behind the content.

    And as AI continues to evolve, from search and answers to emerging agentic experiences, having clear, connected, and reliable business information will only become more key.

    Recent findings suggest that because the goal isn’t just to be found. It’s to be understood. And that starts with taking ownership of the information we control.

    You may already have schema markup. But how well is it communicating the full story of your business?

    Student journalists are reporting more local news for real audiences. Their professors are exhausted.

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3484 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Industry observers note that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    According to recent reports, A fresh study finds that journalism school faculty — charged with putting more student work in front of non-student readers — often serve as a hidden infrastructure for local news. Burnout is a risk.

    If there’s one significant takeaway from the past two decades of local news struggle — the often perilous, occasionally brilliant transition from dominant newspapers to online media — perhaps it’s this: Passion alone isn’t enough.

    A newspaper newsroom filled with committed editors and brilliant reporters still stares into the same headwinds as its more middling peers. The devotion of those leading a nonprofit outlet can mean little if revenue can’t keep the doors open. And even when the money is less vital — when journalism is somewhat protected from the demands of the market — passion is still a finite resource, and it’s not always renewable.

    That truism came to mind when I was reading a recent article by Sima Bhowmik of the University of Vermont and Andrea Lorenz of Kent State. It looks at one specific corner of the contemporary news ecosystem: journalism schools that use their students to fill voids in local coverage.

    J-schools, after all, have faculties full of experience and students who need it. A few decades ago, an early-career journalist might have spent a few years covering city council meetings and school board budgets before moving up the chain to a bigger outlet. That path barely exists these days, and journalism programs know their students need the chance to do real work. What if these reporters-in-training could handle some of the local stories that the city’s daily no longer can?

    According to recent reports, RELATED ARTICLEA “win-win” partnership brings a surge of reporting firepower to hyperlocal news outlets around BostonSarah ScireNovember 13, 2025RELATED ARTICLELen Downie: The teaching hospital model works, but it will require drastic changeLeonard Downie Jr.September 12, 2012If you happen to live near a college with a journalism program, you’ve probably seen this idea — often called the “teaching hospital” model — in action. Here in the Boston suburbs, many of the stories I read about my town are written by Boston University students. According to UVM’s Center for Community News, where Bhowmik is an assistant research professor, there were 282 such efforts as of 2025, producing local news inside 205 colleges and universities. Those numbers were up from 227 programs in 172 colleges the year before — a boom fueled by a surge in philanthropic funding for these partnerships.

    Bhowmik and Lorentz’s paper — published in Journalism & Mass Communication Educator — is the result of interviews with 118 faculty and staff at 101 of those colleges, and their major takeaway is one that will be familiar to many in local news: They’re exhausted.

    Participants repeatedly used phrases such as “at capacity,” “don’t have the bandwidth,” “not enough hours of the day,” and “it’s just a lot” to describe the workload. Several described long workdays and exhaustion, with one participant saying the amount of editing “just about kills me every semester.” At many institutions, faculty workload was intensified by staffing shortages, retirements, hiring freezes, and budget cuts. This left faculty with little time to provide the one-on-one coaching necessary to elevate student stories to publishable quality… “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how important the work is.” (See above: Passion alone isn’t enough.) Here’s how one faculty member described their situation: Think about it: Like, how many reporters does the average assigning editor at a mid-sized newspaper supervise? Half a dozen? So try, like, 20 of them, and each of them is writing for a different outlet maybe, which has its own set of deadlines and editor. And they’re all at varying skill levels, and broadly, they’re all pretty latest. Their copy requires a lot of work, their reporting often requires a lot of handholding. Another talked about the responsibility of getting student work up to the level a news outlet expects. You can’t just give a meh student story a C- and be done with it if a local editor is expecting publishable copy. It takes a lot of work to get student work up to the quality of professionally published work. And a lot of students start out with really good ideas, do some good reporting by the time they’re done in the semester, it needs work, and that tends to fall on the faculty person. And that’s a lot of work outside of uncompensated work…But bridging that gap between what a student produces at the end of a semester and what can actually be published is still a big gap that needs to be addressed. And aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write. Just to save a few dozen proud Mizzou alums from emailing me: Yes, the “teaching hospital” model is not a new idea. The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

    According to recent reports, “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how important the work is.”.

As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

    Recent findings suggest that and aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write.

    Just to save a few dozen proud Mizzou alums from emailing me: Yes, the “teaching hospital” model is not a latest idea.     #32467. Latest Update: How To Find The Questions Your Customers Ask AI (And Your Keyword Tools Miss)

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1813 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: How To Find The Questions Your Customers Ask AI (And Your Keyword Tools Miss)

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that in my last article, I made the case that search volume is screening out your best content opportunities.
    • According to recent reports, so, this is the practical follow-up.
    • I always start here, because it’s the source most teams overlook, and it’s usually the best one.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that in my last article, I made the case that search volume is screening out your best content opportunities. The short version is that the highest-intent questions your buyers ask are increasingly being said to an AI assistant, and they rarely show up in a keyword tool. Near the end of that piece, I listed a few places to find those questions instead: People Also Ask, forums, your own sales calls and support tickets, and the assistants themselves. That list was only four bullet points, and the most common reply I’ve had since is some version of “OK, but how do I actually do that?”.

    According to recent reports, so, this is the practical follow-up. I’ll go through how I collect these questions, how I use Search Console to check which ones are already reaching a site, and how I turn the whole lot into something a content team can work from.

    I always start here, because it’s the source most teams overlook, and it’s usually the best one. Sales calls, discovery calls, support tickets, live chat logs, and the messages people send before booking a demo are all people describing their problem in their own words. That’s very close to how they’d describe it to ChatGPT or Gemini.

    It has been revealed that here’s a real example from a recent discovery call of mine (anonymized, with the details changed enough that you couldn’t identify the business). The prospect was a furniture retailer, and this was roughly how they opened the call:.

    “We moved to Shopify a couple of years ago and lost a major chunk of our rankings. Some of it came back, and then we dropped again this year. Is that still the migration, or are our own collection pages competing with each other?”.

    A few minutes later, they asked a second question:.

    “We sell exactly the same products in France and Germany, but those sites barely get any traffic. Do we need completely separate content for each country?”.

    Industry observers note that neither of those would ever appear in a keyword export. The closest you’d get is something like “shopify migration SEO” or “international SEO,” which tells you almost nothing about the actual situation. But if you look at those two questions as a content brief, they’re incredibly specific: a platform, a timeline, two possible causes, and a decision to make.

    This is exactly the kind of question a buyer takes to an assistant, and it’s the kind of question your content should be able to answer.

    If you record your calls (I use Fireflies, but most call recorders produce a transcript you can export), I’d take the last three months of sales and discovery calls and run them through an AI assistant with a prompt like this:.

    In a recent development, “From these call transcripts, list every question the prospect asked or implied. Rewrite each one the way they would phrase it to an AI assistant, and keep their constraints, such as company size, budget, timeline, platform, and what they’ve already tried. Group similar questions together and note how many calls each group came up in.”.

    In a recent development, the final instruction here is critical. If the same scenario comes up in five separate calls, that’s the closest thing to demand data you’ll get for a question with no search volume, and it’s a lot more persuasive in a meeting than “I think people are asking this.”.

    You want to be careful with a couple of things here. Strip out names, company details, and anything identifying before transcripts go into a third-party tool, and make sure your call recording consent covers this kind of use. Also, sales calls skew toward people who are already close to buying, so I’d add support tickets and pre-sale inquiries into the mix to capture earlier-stage questions too.

    Your own calls only tell you about people who already found you. Forums help with everyone else.

    Industry observers note that reddit is the obvious one, but Quora, industry Slack and Discord communities, Facebook groups, and review sites such as G2 or Trustpilot can all be just as useful depending on your market. The value usually lies in the opening post, where someone explains their constraints in full, and in the replies, where other people ask the follow-up questions an assistant would also need answered before it could give a decent response.

    Sticking with the migration example, a search like site:reddit.com shopify migration rankings dropped should bring up plenty of threads where store owners describe the same problem in their own words, often with details my prospect didn’t mention, such as redirect complications or how long they waited before panicking.

    I copy the most relevant threads into a document and run the same extraction prompt over them. That way, forum questions and sales questions end up in the same format, and you can group them together later.

    See also: The Review Gap: Finding Client Opportunities In Competitor Feedback.

    Once you have a set of real questions, the next step is working out what an AI assistant would actually search for when answering them.

    Google is open about the fact that AI Overviews and AI Mode may use a query fan-out technique, issuing multiple related searches to build a single response. You can’t see those searches for a real AI Mode session, but you can get a reasonable approximation through the Gemini API.

    Industry observers note that when you use Grounding with Google Search, the API response includes a field called webSearchQueries, which lists the searches the model ran to answer your prompt. Google’s own documentation describes it as useful for understanding the model’s reasoning process.

    Recent findings suggest that if you feed in the first migration question from earlier, you’d expect to see sub-queries covering things like how long rankings take to recover after a Shopify migration, how to check redirects after a re-platform, and how to spot keyword cannibalization between collection pages. Your own output will vary from run to run, but each sub-query is effectively a section your page would need to cover to be useful as a source.

    You don’t need to be technical for this. Go Fish Digital published a walkthrough that runs it through Screaming Frog with a copy-and-paste custom JavaScript snippet and an API key from Google AI Studio. Their version sends each page’s H1, but swapping in your own list of questions is straightforward.

    I want to be clear about what this output is, though. It shows you how a Gemini model expands a question, which is a fair proxy for Google’s AI features, but it isn’t a record of what AI Mode ran for an actual user. I treat it as a coverage checklist, and I wouldn’t present it to a client as anything more definitive than that.

    According to recent reports, for ChatGPT, Perplexity, and the other assistants, the manual route still works fine. Ask each one your question, note which sub-topics it decides to cover and which sources it cites, and compare that against the page that’s supposed to answer it.

    See also: The 2003 Framework That Was Already Doing Query Fan-Out.

    Search Console is better as a validation step than a discovery tool for this, because it shows you which of these questions are already finding their way to your site.

    Long conversational queries do turn up in the Performance report. Suganthan Mohanadasan has already covered four ways to surface them in a lot of detail, so I’d recommend checking that out if you haven’t already. For a quick look, I use the Custom (regex) option in the Query filter. This pattern returns queries of eight words or more:.

    And this one returns queries that start with a question word:.

    Sources indicate that then I compare what comes back against the questions from calls and forums. If the migration scenario indicates up as a long query, that’s good confirmation that real people are bringing it to Google. If it doesn’t show up, it could be a coverage gap, or the queries may simply be too rare for Google to show you.

    That last point is significant because Google anonymizes rare queries, and conversational queries are rare almost by definition. Suganthan found that 57.7% of his impressions sat in the anonymized pool over a 59-day period, so anything you find here is an undercount.

    According to recent reports, if you have access to the generative AI performance report, the pages view is worth a look too. It shows which of your URLs are already appearing in AI Overviews and AI Mode. There’s no query data in it (yet), and sites with few AI impressions may not see the report at all, but it does tell you which pages Google is already comfortable using as a source.

    By now, you’ll have a messy list of questions from several sources. To get it into a shape a content team can actually use, I put everything into one sheet. Here’s how a single row might look, using the migration example:.

    For the priority column, I use the same proxies from my previous column: business value, evidence that the question is being asked, how significant the coverage gap is, and whether you can answer it with real specifics. The frequency column feeds straight into the second one.

    Once the sheet is filled in, you’ll usually notice that most of the questions cluster around a handful of situations. Those clusters are your content plan. In my experience, most of them can be handled by strengthening a page you already have, which is quicker than publishing something fresh and tends to perform better too.

    I’m aware this is a lot less tidy than sorting a spreadsheet by volume, so I think it’s worth being up front about the limitations.

    You still won’t have a volume figure next to any of these questions, which means you’re prioritizing on judgment and frequency. Your own calls are biased toward people who already know you exist, so questions from audiences you don’t reach yet will be underrepresented. The Gemini fan-out is an approximation of Google’s behavior, and Search Console only reveals you part of the picture because of anonymization.

    However, I don’t think any of that is a reason not to do it. It just means you should present the output as a well-evidenced shortlist, particularly to stakeholders who are used to seeing a number next to every target or goal.

    If you want somewhere to start right now:.

    Keyword tools are still useful for understanding what people type into a search box. But a growing share of the questions that decide whether a buyer picks you are being asked in a conversation with an assistant, and the good news is that plenty of them are already sitting in your inbox and call recordings.

    Lisa Sygutek, publisher of the Crowsnest Pass Herald in Alberta, credited the LJI with growing the publication from “a 16-page paper to a 24-page paper.”.
